openingProblem.problem: In 1934 the party congress hailed Stalin as the leader of a victorious revolution. Within four years more than half its delegates had been arrested, and hundreds of thousands of ordinary citizens had been shot. Why did Stalin's regime turn on its own party and people, and how did it keep their loyalty at the same time?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: terror, belief, or both?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: From the Congress of Victors to Kirov's murder, 1934
chunks.body:
By 1934 Stalin's victory over the oppositions seemed complete. At the **Seventeenth Party Congress** in January–February 1934, the "Congress of Victors", former oppositionists praised him and delegates celebrated a good harvest and new factories. Yet some historians claim that regional party secretaries privately discussed replacing Stalin with **Sergei Kirov**, the popular Leningrad party leader. The evidence for this, and for reports that Stalin received fewer votes than Kirov, is thin. What is certain is grim: within four years, 1,108 of the 1,966 delegates had been arrested, and most disappeared into the Gulag or were shot.

On **1 December 1934** Kirov was shot dead in Leningrad by Leonid Nikolaev, a frustrated party official. Stalin personally supervised the investigation and quickly blamed supporters of Zinoviev. Zinoviev, Kamenev and many associates were arrested. Many western historians long believed that Stalin had arranged the murder himself to justify a terror against the party. But investigations in the 1960s and in 1989 failed to prove his complicity, and Lewis Siegelbaum judges the link between the murder and the later Terror "more circumstantial than direct".

The murder nevertheless created an atmosphere of vigilance and suspicion. Secret police reports on public reactions show that many ordinary people cared more about food shortages than politics, and some even hoped Stalin would share Kirov's fate.

This mattered because Kirov's murder gave Stalin a pretext to treat former opponents as terrorists, which meant that the Terror could be presented as the defence of the state.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin's position in 1934 was strong but not unquestioned.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Evidence of a plot against him is thin.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Kirov's murder gave Stalin a pretext.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His complicity has not been proved.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ordinary people were not loyal enthusiasts.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Kirov became a martyr in the party.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Kirov's murder was significant as a pretext rather than as a cause of the Terror.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Stalin blamed supporters of Zinoviev for the shooting of 1 December 1934, and Zinoviev and Kamenev were arrested and later put on trial in 1936.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that former oppositionists could be treated as terrorists, so a political defeat became a criminal charge.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, investigations in the 1960s and 1989 failed to prove Stalin arranged the murder, and Siegelbaum calls its link to the Terror circumstantial.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Kirov's murder therefore opened the way to the Terror without explaining why it reached the scale it did.

chunks.title: The Great Terror, 1936–1938
chunks.body:
The **Great Terror** of 1936–38, also called the Ezhovshchina after the secret police chief Nikolai **Ezhov**, was a wave of state-organised killing that swept through the party and society. Its public face was three **show trials** of former leaders. In August 1936 Zinoviev, Kamenev and fourteen others were convicted of forming a terrorist centre. In September Stalin replaced the NKVD chief Iagoda with Ezhov. Piatakov and other economic leaders were tried in January 1937. In March 1938 Bukharin, Rykov and Iagoda himself were sentenced to death.

Behind the trials, arrests spread far wider. The leadership of the **Red Army** was devastated, as were provincial party secretaries, industrial managers and officials among the national minorities. Prisoners, under severe physical and psychological pressure, named others and confessed to absurd crimes. On **3 July 1937** the Politburo ordered "mass operations" against ex-kulaks, criminals and other "anti-Soviet elements". Ezhov set quotas for each district, 177,500 to be exiled and 72,950 shot, and these were exceeded.

Official figures record **681,692 executions** in 1937 and 1938, and estimates of total deaths range from about 950,000 to 1.2 million. Nobody at the top could stop it: Siegelbaum notes that no important issue was decided by the Politburo without Stalin, "and certainly not against his will", and in 1937 a small inner circle of Stalin, Molotov and Kaganovich replaced the full Politburo.

This mattered because the Terror destroyed the party's old elite and spread fear through society, which meant that by 1939 Stalin ruled over a party, army and state whose leaders owed everything to him.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The show trials destroyed the old Bolsheviks.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The accused confessed to invented crimes.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Mass operations extended the Terror to society.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some historians stress pressures from below.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Great Terror destroyed any possible alternative to Stalin's rule.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Three show trials between 1936 and 1938 condemned Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin and Rykov, while the army's leadership and provincial party secretaries were decimated.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the generation who had known Stalin as an equal was eliminated, so those who remained owed their positions to him.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the mass operations ordered in July 1937 struck ex-kulaks and 'anti-Soviet elements' far beyond the elite, which suggests the Terror had wider aims.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Terror therefore secured Stalin's personal power while spreading fear through the whole of society.

chunks.title: Propaganda, the constitution and the cult
chunks.body:
Terror was not Stalin's only instrument. The regime also tried to win belief. In **August 1934** the First Congress of Soviet Writers declared **socialist realism** the method of Soviet literature: art had to be accessible, rooted in the people and loyal to the party, and its heroes increasingly included Stalin himself.

In **December 1936**, in the middle of the Terror, the regime adopted the "**Stalin Constitution**". It gave all citizens equal rights and the vote, including former kulaks and priests, and its draft was officially discussed at 623,334 meetings attended by over 42 million people. It did not prevent arbitrary repression, but later protesters would appeal to its words against the state.

By the end of the 1930s the **cult of personality** was in full swing. Historians rewrote party history to place Stalin at its centre; the *Short Course* history of the party, published in 1938, sold forty million copies. Stalin Prizes rewarded loyal achievement from 1939, and strong rulers of the Russian past such as Peter the Great were rehabilitated as models. During the war Stalin admired Eisenstein's film of Ivan the Terrible, awarding part one a Stalin Prize in 1944, then condemned part two in 1946.

This mattered because propaganda gave the regime a positive image of strong leadership and a happy socialist society, which meant that terror and belief worked together rather than as alternatives.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Socialist realism made culture serve the party.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It took many forms in practice.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1936 Constitution offered rights on paper.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It did not stop the Terror.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The cult placed Stalin at the centre of history.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It drew on Russian traditions of strong rule.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Propaganda gave Stalin's rule a positive face that terror alone could not.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The 1936 Constitution was discussed at 623,334 meetings, and the Short Course of 1938 sold forty million copies and placed Stalin at the centre of party history.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that citizens were offered an image of rights, progress and wise leadership, so loyalty could rest on belief as well as fear.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Constitution did not prevent the Terror, and NKVD reports show many people cared more about food than politics.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Propaganda was therefore important in building Stalin's authority, but it worked alongside terror rather than replacing it.

chunks.title: Post-war Stalinism and the historians' debate, 1945–1953
chunks.body:
Victory in 1945 did not bring relaxation. Of five and a half million Soviet citizens repatriated by 1953, one in five was shot or sent to the Gulag. From 1946 to 1948 the **zhdanovshchina**, led by Andrei Zhdanov, tightened ideological control: in August 1946 the journals *Zvezda* and *Leningrad* were attacked for publishing the satirist Zoshchenko and the poet Akhmatova, and a campaign against "cosmopolitanism" followed. A 1947 law banned marriage to foreigners, and almost all information became a state secret. In 1948 Lysenko's victory halted genetic research. After Zhdanov's death that August, a purge struck thousands of Leningrad officials. In January 1953 nine eminent doctors, many of them Jewish, were accused of plotting to poison the Soviet leadership. Only Stalin's death on **5 March 1953** stopped the "Doctors' Plot"; the new leaders declared it a fabrication.

How far was Stalin personally responsible for the terror? The opening of the archives has strengthened the case against him. Oleg **Khlevniuk** says theories of a spontaneous, uncontrolled terror "are simply not supported by the historical record": Stalin signed 357 lists in 1937–38 authorising the execution of about 40,000 people. Revisionists such as Robert W. **Thurston** argue that Stalin initiated or reacted to events rather than acting as a "cold mastermind", and that the purge was aimed at elite opposition. Robert Conquest's estimate of about one million executions is broadly supported by the official figure of 681,692 for 1937–38, while J. Arch Getty stresses that the archives rule out the highest estimates.

This mattered because terror remained central to Stalin's rule until his death, which meant that the debate among historians is about the degree of his control, not whether repression was systematic.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: There was no return to mass terror on the 1937 scale.
The Doctors' Plot ended with his death.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Archives strengthen the case for Stalin's responsibility.

howItGetsAsked: Compare and contrast Stalin's methods of control before and after the Second World War, between 1934 and 1953.
“Stalin was personally responsible for the Great Terror.” Discuss with reference to the period 1936 to 1938.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Stalin's methods after 1945 continued those of the 1930s in a narrower form.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Zhdanov's attack of August 1946 on Zoshchenko and Akhmatova renewed control of culture, and the Doctors' Plot of January 1953 revived the language of conspiracy.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that ideological discipline and the search for enemies remained central, so the post-war years brought no relaxation.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, there was no repeat of the mass operations of 1937–38, and the Doctors' Plot was dropped after Stalin's death.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Post-war Stalinism therefore kept the methods of the 1930s while applying terror more selectively.

Result: an inner circle loyal to Stalin.

modelPlan.counter: Harris argues the Terror was driven by fear of counter-revolution rather than personal dictatorship.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result mattered most? A party and army whose leaders owed everything to Stalin.

segments.text: The Great Terror arose mainly from Stalin's determination to remove any possible rival.
After doubts surfaced at the 1934 Congress, 1,108 of its 1,966 delegates were arrested within four years, and three show trials destroyed Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin.
This meant that every leader who had known Stalin as an equal was removed, so by 1939 the party and army were led by men who owed him everything.
However, James Harris argues the Terror was driven by an exaggerated fear of counter-revolution, and the mass operations struck far beyond the elite.
The most significant result was therefore Stalin's unchallengeable power, bought at the cost of the army's leadership on the eve of war.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast Stalin's methods of control before and after the Second World War, between 1934 and 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout

modelPlan.thesis: Stalin's methods showed strong continuity, terror, propaganda and the search for enemies, but after 1945 repression was more selective, aimed at returning citizens, intellectuals and foreign influence rather than at mass operations on the scale of 1937–38.

arguments.claim: Difference: mass operations versus selective repression.

modelPlan.counter: The Doctors' Plot may have been the prelude to a new wave of terror, stopped only by Stalin's death.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Continuity or change? Continuity of methods, change of scale and targets.

segments.text: Stalin's methods after 1945 continued those of the 1930s, but in a more selective form.
In the 1930s mass operations ordered in July 1937 struck hundreds of thousands, whereas after 1945 repression targeted repatriated citizens, writers such as Akhmatova and, in 1953, Jewish doctors.
This meant that the search for enemies remained central, but its targets shifted from former oppositionists to foreign influence and 'cosmopolitanism'.
However, both periods relied on invented conspiracies, from the charge that Zinoviev's supporters killed Kirov to the Doctors' Plot.
The methods were therefore continuous, while the scale and targets of repression changed after the war.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the purposes of the show trials held between 1936 and 1938.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which purpose mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The show trials eliminated Stalin's former rivals, blamed economic and political failures on 'enemies', and justified the wider Terror by presenting it as the defence of the state against conspiracy.

arguments.claim: Linking the opposition to Kirov's murder.

modelPlan.counter: The trials were a small, public part of a Terror that mostly took place in secret.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which purpose mattered most? Removing rivals, which the other purposes justified.

segments.text: The show trials served above all to destroy Stalin's former rivals in a way that justified their destruction.
Zinoviev and Kamenev were convicted in 1936 of forming a terrorist centre blamed for Kirov's murder, and Bukharin and Rykov were sentenced to death in 1938.
This meant that former leaders confessed publicly to treason, so their elimination appeared as the defence of the state rather than a political purge.
However, the trials were only the public face of a far wider secret Terror, including the mass operations of 1937.
The trials therefore removed rivals and provided the justification for repression on a much larger scale.
